questions.q: Identify the grammatical mood of the opening line "Let me not to the marriage of true minds / Admit impediments" and state its function in the poem.
questions.a: The opening line uses the imperative mood ("Let me not") to frame the poem as a formal declaration or vow. A wrong answer (e.g., "indicative mood" or "subjunctive") reveals the student cannot distinguish mood types or see how the imperative establishes the speaker's authority to define love.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the poet uses a series of negatives ("not," "nor," "never," "no") to define love instead of positive statements.
questions.a: The negatives create a definition by exclusion: love is defined by what it does *not* do (alter, bend, end). This makes the positive assertion ("ever-fixed mark," "star") more forceful. A wrong answer (e.g., "to make the poem sound sad") shows the student misses the rhetorical strategy of *via negativa* and its link to the theme of constancy.

questions.q: In the line "Love's not Time's fool," identify the grammatical subject, the complement, and the figure of speech. Then rewrite the line in modern standard English without changing the meaning.
questions.a: Subject: "Love" (personified abstract noun). Complement: "Time's fool" (metaphorical noun phrase). Figure of speech: Personification (both Love and Time) + Metaphor. Modern rewrite: "Love is not the plaything of Time." A wrong answer that misses personification or misidentifies the complement shows the student cannot parse the clause or see the double personification.

questions.q: Compare the two metaphor clusters in the poem (navigation: "star," "wandering bark," "compass," "height"; harvest/time: "bending sickle," "compass," "brief hours and weeks"). How does the grammar of each cluster (noun phrases, possessives, prepositional phrases) reinforce the poem's argument?
questions.a: The navigation cluster uses static, measuring language ("height be taken," "ever-fixed mark") suggesting permanence; the time cluster uses dynamic, limiting language ("bending sickle's compass," "brief hours") suggesting transience. The grammar contrasts stasis vs. motion. A wrong answer that only lists metaphors without analyzing grammatical form reveals the student cannot link syntax to thematic contrast.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the final couplet's double negative ("If this be error and upon me proved, / I never writ, nor no man ever loved") as a logical proof. Does the archaic grammar strengthen or weaken the argument for a modern reader?
questions.a: The double negative ("never writ, nor no man ever loved") creates a logical impossibility: if the poem is wrong, then no poetry exists and no love has ever existed — an absurdity that proves the poem's truth. The archaic grammar (negative concord) intensifies the absolute claim. A wrong answer that calls it "confusing" or "incorrect grammar" shows the student judges by modern prescriptive rules instead of recognizing rhetorical deliberate use.

questions.q: Write two original sentences that imitate the poem's grammatical strategy: (a) use an imperative to make a declaration about an abstract concept, (b) use a negative definition (listing what the concept is *not*) followed by a positive metaphor.
questions.a: Example: (a) "Let no voice deny the power of truth." (b) "Courage is not fear's absence, nor does it flee when danger looms; it is the lighthouse standing firm in the storm." A poor answer that uses only positive statements or misses the imperative/negative pattern shows the student cannot transfer the grammatical strategy to new content.
